doc:
/**
 * Week 4 — the spellings that survive to the final exam.
 *
 * -ance against -ence, -ary against -ery against -ory, the doubled consonants
 * nobody hears (accommodation, occurrence, embarrass), the Greek and French
 * borrowings that kept their own spelling (psychology, technique, colleague,
 * rhythm), and the silent letters that only survive in a handful of words.
 *
 * Three deliberate pairs run through the week because they are the ones that
 * cost marks in an exam and nowhere else: `stationary`/`stationery`,
 * `practice`/`practise`, and `breath`/`breathe`. Each is a real distinction a
 * confident speaker still gets wrong in writing, which is precisely what this
 * programme exists to fix.
 *
 * The sentences here are the hardest in the corpus: conditionals, reported
 * speech and relative clauses, because by day 28 a learner is being examined
 * on construction as well as spelling.
 */

days.title: Ance and ence
days.focus: Two endings that sound identical, and the words that take each.

days.title: Ary, ery, ory
days.focus: Stationary against stationery, and the -ary endings that lose a syllable when spoken.

days.title: Doubles nobody hears
days.focus: Accommodation, occurrence, embarrass — where the doubling is invisible in speech.

days.title: Words English borrowed
days.focus: Greek ch and ps, French -que and -gue: technique, psychology, colleague.

days.title: The last silent letters
days.focus: Column, muscle, hymn, resign — the letters that survive in only a few words.

days.title: Long verbs and their forms
days.focus: -ate verbs, the -ceed/-cede split, and doubling on a stressed final syllable.

days.title: Everything at once
days.focus: Conditionals, reported speech and relative clauses — construction as well as spelling.
